headline: Committee presented initial budget-cut and revenue ideas, including health insurance cost sharing, parking fee increases, camp fees, and pension payment deferral.
summary: This document is a slide presentation for a community meeting, not minutes. It presents initial ideas for budget reductions and new revenue, with estimated financial impacts and next steps for each. It records no votes or decisions.

Special Committee on Deficit Reduction 
(Deficit Reduction Committee)
Community Meeting #1
 
October 20, 2026
Beverly Council on Aging
6:00pm - 7:30pm
Agenda
● Purpose and Format of Tonight’s Meeting
● Background on the Establishment and Role of the Special 
Committee on Deficit Reduction
● Introductions to Committee Members
● Initial Ideas Reviewed
● Questions and Answers
● Next Steps
Purpose and Format of Tonight’s Meeting
● The purpose of tonight’s meeting is for the Committee to present its initial work and research 
to the public. The Committee has been working to gather information, evaluate ideas, and 
provide recommendations. Decisions regarding policy are made by the appropriate governing 
and decision-making bodies.
● Committee members will briefly present each idea that has been reviewed to date and provide 
some preliminary information on topics such as potential financial impacts and considerations 
such as pros and cons.
● At the end of the presentation, the Committee welcomes questions and feedback from the 
public. Please add your name to the sign-up sheet if you would like to speak, and a member 
of the committee will call on you in turn. The Committee values community input and is 
especially interested in learning about additional information, opportunities, or ideas that could 
explored as part of this effort. 
● The Committee views this meeting as an initial public meeting. Additional meetings are 
anticipated to be scheduled this fall and winter.
Background on the Establishment and Role of the Special Committee on 
Deficit Reduction
● In January 2026, Councilors Feldman and Mullady proposed the creation of the 
committee to the City Council. The committee establishment was subsequently approved 
by the City Council. 
● Committee goals include examining potential approaches for increasing budget flexibility 
and operational efficiencies; assessing impacts on residents and services; further 
exploring increased revenue generation; and identifying best practices from comparable 
communities. 
● On June 15, 2026, the City Council voted to approve Committee appointments following 
an advertised membership application process. 
● The Committee convened its work on July 20, 2026 and currently meets bimonthly.
Introductions to Committee Members
● Lydia Ames
● Christine DePalma
● Kathleen Feldman, City Council Representative
● Dan Hughes
● Madeline Lennox, School Committee Member
● John Mullady, City Council Representative 
● Mark Munoz
● Kaarin Robinson, School Committee Member
Photo Credit: The Salem News
Ideas Reviewed To Date
● At its initial meetings this past summer, Committee members brainstormed potential 
ideas for budget reductions and revenue generation. Ideas shared by members of the 
public were also reviewed. 
● Committee members volunteered to take the lead on researching the ideas. This 
involved talking with subject matter experts from the City, talking with other 
municipalities, learning more about how the state budget process works from 
Representative Bowen, and completing some initial benchmarking research. 
● The following slides highlight ideas that have been studied to date and will be presented 
by Committee members. The Committee generally has an approach to leave no stone 
unturned!
Pension Deferral
Contributor: Dan Hughes
Proposal Level load pension obligation payment until statutory requirement.
Financial impact Overall, no long-term impact but will save cash requirements every year.
Timing ASAP
Considerations Market overperformance has allowed us to keep pension obligation
payments flat until 2030.
Next steps Monitor market performance and make proper adjustments.
Regional Dispatch
Contributor: Dan Hughes
Proposal Move Beverly Civilian Dispatch to Middleton Regional Dispatch
Financial impact $400,000 to $600,000 (planning level estimate)
Timing 2+ years
Considerations Cost saving vs. citizen benefits; we learned that the Beverly Police dispatch 
space was built with some room for growth. 
Next steps Currently no capacity at the Middleton facility, they would be looking to
expand in a few years. No current opportunity for the City.
Health Insurance - Employees and City Cost Share
Contributor: Dan Hughes
Proposal Change the cost sharing from 80/20 to 70/30
Financial impact $1,500,000 (approximate estimate)
Timing Pursuant to current labor negotiations.
Considerations Brings Beverly in line with surrounding communities
Next steps Any changes need to be negotiated with each union. Contracts are
renewed in 2027.
Health Insurance - Retirees and City Cost Share
Contributor: Dan Hughes
Proposal Bring retirees insurance cost sharing to state minimum 50/50.
Financial impact $2,000,000 (approximate estimate)
Timing At any point or on new open enrollment period.
Considerations State minimum for retirees shared cost is 50/50 where Beverly still pays
80/20.
Next steps This would need to be addressed by Mayor and approved by Council.
Join Group Insurance Commission (GIC) or Massachusetts Interlocal 
Insurance Association (MIAA)
Contributor: Dan Hughes
Proposal Moving from self-insured into the GIC or MIAA
Financial impact $400,000 to $1,600,000 if cost sharing changes
Timing Change during new open enrollment cycle.
Considerations Less control over trust investing activities. Less hassle for the city to
administer self-insurance.
Next steps Need to be discussed in Mayor’s budget meetings and approved by City 
Council.
PILOTS (Payments in Lieu of Taxes)
Contributor: Kaarin Robinson
Proposal Develop larger, multi-year voluntary contributions from Beverly’s tax-exempt institutions through a 
community partnership initiative. 
● Additional potential revenue has not been estimated. Confirm current contributions, property 
values, and potential commitments before setting a target.
● Costs would include staff time for research, negotiations, and agreement administration.
● Boston benchmark: 25% (Read about it here: 
https://www.boston.gov/departments/assessing/payment-lieu-tax-pilot-program)
Begin research and institutional meetings this fall. Explore agreements for FY2028 budget 
planning, subject to negotiations.
Distinguish voluntary donations, negotiated PILOT contributions, and required housing authority 
payments. Establish consistent expectations and recognize existing community contributions.
● Continue the tax-exempt property research with City staff
● Follow up with Hannah Bowen on shared materials and earlier Beverly PILOT work.
● Committee leadership: arrange introductory meetings with institutional leaders.
Financial impact
Timing
Considerations
Next steps
SILOTS (Services in Lieu of Taxes)
Contributor: Madeline Lennox
Proposal Include defined services in the community partnership discussions. Earlier proposals included 
student teaching, Beverly High internships, workforce development, affordable youth hockey ice 
time, and community access to facilities.
Identify services Beverly currently pays for that a partner could provide, then estimate the actual 
avoided cost. Track broader community benefits separately from budget savings.
Develop service options alongside PILOT negotiations. Start with a small number of clearly 
defined commitments.
Services need measurable value, reliable delivery, and clear beneficiaries. Internships and 
expanded access provide community benefits but may not directly reduce city spending. Establish 
how service commitments would relate to cash contributions.
● Develop education and internship partnership options.
● School and city staff: identify needs and estimate potential savings.
● Institutional representatives: propose specific services, capacity, and delivery schedules.
Financial impact
Timing
Considerations
Next steps
Enterprise Funds
● An enterprise fund in Beverly is a separate, self‑contained account the city uses for services that 
operate like a business — meaning they charge user fees and track their own revenues and expenses 
independently from the general city budget. This structure is defined under M.G.L. c. 44, §53F½ and is 
used widely across Massachusetts. 
● Enterprise funds: 
○ Keep all revenues and costs for a specific service in its own account, separate from the general 
fund.
○ Show the full cost of running that service — including salaries, insurance, debt service, and capital 
expenses.
○ Allow the city to set user fees that reflect actual operating costs.
○ Allow any surplus to become retained earnings.
Contributor: Lydia Ames
Camp and Recreation Fees
Contributor: Lydia Ames
Proposal Monetize the current free parks program held at Beverly park locations
Financial impact In the summer of 2026, 753 children registered for the park program and 
approximately 288 attended daily. 
Option A: If we implemented a registration fee of $20 at the start of the 
summer, we could generate $15,000 dollars of revenue. 
Option B: If we implemented a daily fee of $2 a day, we could generate 
$23,000. A daily fee of $5 could generate $57,000.
Timing This change could be made at the start of summer 2027.  
Considerations Changing a park from a “drop off camp” to a “day camp” (option B) requires 
changes in staffing (staff aged 19+) and access to bathrooms, which not all 
parks currently have. How will fees affect enrollment? Recreation department 
is currently an Enterprise fund. 
Next steps Add to DRC recommendations. If approved, look at registration fees in other 
cities and research changes needed in staffing/facilities
Camp and Recreation Fees
Contributor: Lydia Ames
Proposal Expand the paid “day camp” program at Lynch park or create additional 
locations at Ober park
Financial impact In the summer of 2025, a new day camp program “Endless Summer” was 
started. It had 30 participants, but in the summer of 2026 it expanded to 50 
participants and a waiting list. It generated revenue of $14,000. If each 
participant is generating $280 of revenue, expanding the camp size at Lynch 
Park or hosting a camp at Ober park could generate more. 
Timing This change could be made at the start of summer 2027.  
Considerations Does Ober park have the structural supports necessary to host a day camp?
What impact will two camp locations have on resources?
Is expanding the staff and offerings feasible?
Next steps Add to DRC recommendations. If approved, research the upfront costs (if they 
exist) to support the expansion
Parking Fees/General Increase
Contributor: Mark Munoz
Proposal Increase the hourly parking rate in the current parking zones
Financial impact Current rate of $1.00/hour generates an estimate $400k / year. Raising the 
rate to $2.00 could generate an additional $400k annually. Annual parking 
enforcement expenses are ~$180,000. Annual violations are ~$275,000.
Timing The changes could be made at any time once approved.
Considerations The potential impact to downtown businesses would need to be understood. 
The city could also look at establishing a parking benefit district, which could 
provide a benefit to certain downtown areas.
Next steps Review any potential impact on downtown businesses and / or residents. Add 
to the list of DRC recommendations.
Parking Fees: Meter Zone Expansion
Contributor: Mark Munoz
Proposal Add parking meter zones along Lothrop St from Independence Park to Dane 
Street Beach.
Financial impact 180 parking spots could generate $470,000 to $1.8M a year, assuming 
enforcement from 8 AM to 8 PM. 
Timing If the city used the AP only method for payment, adding signage and zones is 
all that would be needed to start very quickly. If the city also wants to offer 
kiosks, that takes more time to order and install ($14k each.)
Considerations Would need to look at any impact to residents, and how those could be 
mitigated. 
Next steps Add to list of DRC recommendations. If approved, look further in to resident 
impact and potential mitigation steps.
Miscellaneous Fees
Contributor: Mark Munoz
Proposal Formalize the process and frequency that the city council uses to review all 
city fees 
Financial impact Would vary widely depending on which fees, if any, were increased or 
decreased.
Timing If approved by the city council the review process could be implemented 
quickly, possibly becoming part of the annual budget review.
Considerations The review process would need to include the financial impact on 
stakeholders (residents, businesses, builders etc)
Next steps Add to the list of DRC recommendations.
Golf Course
Contributor: Mark Munoz
Proposal Look for opportunities to increase revenue to the city from BG&T
Financial impact No meaningful current opportunities. BG&T is managed by an outside 
company for an annual flat fee paid to the city.
Timing N/A
Considerations BG&T is an enterprise fund. As such the fee paid to the city goes back in to 
the enterprise fund and does not contribute to the general fund in a 
meaningful way.
Next steps No current DRC opportunity. The contract runs through 2029, so possibly the 
city could investigate other opportunities to implement at that time.
Harbor
Contributor: Mark Munoz
Proposal Increase certain Harbormaster fees. Current annual revenue ~$125k, mainly 
from various mooring fees
Financial impact Current mooring fee is $7 /ft. Every $1 increase would add an estimated $15k 
to the city general fund. 
Timing Rates were reviewed and increased ($5.50-$7.00) last year. Prior to that it had 
been at least 10 years since last rate adjustment. 
Considerations Current waitlist for moorings is about 100, average wait is 3-5 years. Salem 
mooring fee is $7, Danvers is $5, Marblehead is $13
Next steps Add to the list of DRC recommendations.
Harbor Management Authority
Contributor: Mark Munoz
Proposal Increase revenue from Glover Wharf through BHMA
Financial impact No current opportunity 
Timing N/A
Considerations BHMA was set up by the State and sits outside city government. All fees 
collected stay within BHMA and support the related infrastructure. 
Next steps No current DRC opportunity.
Airport
Contributor: John Mullady
Proposal Increase Landing Fees and Refueling Fees at Beverly Airport
Financial impact TBD, Financial Impact would mean more money into the Airport Enterprise 
Fund
Timing TBD
Considerations Impact on Airport Use, Noise with Neighbors
Next steps Discussions with Airport Commission
Municipal Electric
Contributor: John Mullady
Proposal Beverly will switch to a Municipal Light Structure 
Financial impact There would be an initial cost to buyout National Grid,
Savings would be to the residents with lower electric rates 
Timing Varies
Considerations Initial cost of buying out National Grid
Establishing a Municipal Light Company and Municipal Light Board
Next steps City Council would need to allocate funding for a consultant to conduct a 
feasibility study
Override
Contributor: Lydia Ames
Proposal A Proposition 2 ½ override is something that could be voted on in the future. It 
would be put on a ballot and the residents of Beverly would decide. 
Financial impact Would be determined by the dollar amount or percentage increase that was 
voted on.
Timing An override question could be added to the November 2027 municipal 
elections
Considerations It would need to be made very clear what specifically the override was being 
used for. There can be exemptions to an override. For example, a property 
value threshold, as well as for financial hardship. 
Next steps Research overrides in surrounding cities. Determine the override amount(s) 
for citizen voting. Use override calculators to understand estimate impact to 
residents. Read more here: 
https://www.mass.gov/info-details/proposition-2-12-overrides-exclusions
https://dls-gw.dor.state.ma.us/reports/rdPage.aspx?rdReport=Analysis.TaxImpactCalc
Chapter 70
Contributor: Lydia Ames
Impact Chapter 70 is a formula that is used to calculate the foundation budget of a 
school district and the ability for the city to fund the budget for all students.
The formula does take into consideration the median income of the 
community, but a bigger consideration is made to property values.
Beverly (along with about half of all MA communities) is considered a 
“minimum aid” city, meaning, minimum funding.
Timing A committee is forming in 2028 to research and recommend changes to the 
Chapter 70 formula. The Governor has proposed a one time payout of State Aid 
to mitigate the struggles facing communities but that is currently stalled.
Next steps The city should continue to seek ways to reach out to stakeholders and elected 
officials at the State Level to encourage changes to current structures.
Center for Hard-to-Recycle Materials (CHaRM) Facility
Contributor: Christine DePalma
Proposal Establishing a CHaRM facility to benefit residents by reducing landfill waste. 
Items such as electronics, mattresses, textiles, batteries, and certain plastics 
would be diverted from the waste stream. It is also possible that the facility could 
generate revenue over time.
Financial impact Start up and operational costs for infrastructure needs and staffing. 
Timing The City is currently applying for grants to start up a facility. If the grants are 
awarded, it is possible to start a facility in the near future. 
Considerations There is no current funding available for this. Grants are short term opportunities 
but will help! 
Next steps Understand if the Mayor and city policy makers believe this is a priority to 
advance and if funding beyond grant funding would be available for sustaining 
operations.
Other Ideas Beginning to Be Studied
● Shared Regional Services 
● Audit of non-healthcare insurance
● Audit of School efficiencies 
● Potential sale of Hurd and/or Cooney fields
● City vehicles and personal use policy
● Other sustainable initiatives to help reduce trash output such as pet waste composting
● Increasing cannabis retail (per what is already approved for zoning)
Benchmarking Data
● The Committee is compiling 
benchmarking data to evaluate ideas it 
is studying against those implemented 
in comparable municipalities. 
● 26 municipalities have been identified 
by City staff. Not all of them are direct 
peers to each aspect of our community 
and how we operate but each offers 
useful insights.
● Benchmarking provides valuable 
context, helps identify potential proven 
strategies to consider, and may allow 
the Committee and City policymakers 
to learn from others as we move 
forward.
Next Steps
● The Committee will review feedback 
received and follow-up on questions and 
ideas that require further review. 
● The Committee will plan future meetings 
with the community this fall and winter. 
These meetings may be designed as focus 
groups or listening sessions. We will publish 
the dates and locations for these meetings 
in the near future.
● We want to continue the conversation with 
the public in between meetings too. Please 
reach out to committee members or the City 
Council representatives with any questions 
or feedback that you may have. 
Draft Schedule
Questions and Answers
● The Committee welcomes your feedback, 
ideas, and questions! Committee 
members are volunteers and not 
policymakers.
● If you have a question or feedback, 
please raise your hand and a member of 
the committee will call on you. The 
Committee is especially interested in any 
additional information about any of the 
ideas presented that could be further 
studied and also in any new ideas. 
● The Committee may not have answers to 
all questions but we will do our best to 
address them.
